title: Does weight-sharing lookup-table inference beat an int8 MAC engine once small arrays cost less to read?
lede: pricing every array by its own size flips accel-lut's negative result once read energy grows faster than size^0.26 (dense) or size^0.28 (pruned); Horowitz's slope is 0.5 above 8 KB but there is no point below it, so the verdict is conditional
summary: accel-lut found a product-table engine loses to an int8 MAC engine (about 2.7× the energy within a 2-point accuracy drop) while charging every array a flat 0.16 pJ/bit. accel-horowitzcheck showed that flat read ignores array size. This project prices each array (weights or indices, activation buffer, the 32-byte product table) as (10 pJ/64) (size/8 KB)α per bit, keeping accel-lut's accuracy and nonzero counts. The cheapest design within tolerance ties the MAC at α = 0.26 (dense) and 0.28 (75% pruned); at α = 0.5, the slope of Horowitz's Fig. 1.1.9 between 8 and 32 KB, it uses 0.52 and 0.68 of the MAC's energy. Every array here is below 8 KB, where the paper has no data, so α is swept rather than chosen and the flip is conditional; a model that never prices arrays below the 8 KB point reproduces the original negative result. Next step: measure small arrays in an open PDK.
